scenario: Deuce court, 40-15. You've won three straight points serving wide, but on that last one the returner started a metre wider and took it early crosscourt. Where do you serve now?
options: Serve T into the space they left
Serve wide again, harder this time
Serve at their body to jam them
explanation: They have shown the adjustment — a metre wider and stepping in — so the T they abandoned is now free space. Serving wide again with more pace fires straight into the ball they just repositioned to hit.
takeaway: Repeat a winning serve until they move, then serve where they moved from.

scenario: Ad court, 30-15. Your wide serve is blocked back deep and heavy into your backhand corner, and you're a metre behind the baseline still recovering. What's the +1?
options: Heavy backhand crosscourt and reset
Run around it for an inside-out forehand
Backhand down the line into the open court
explanation: A deep return kills the +1, so height and depth crosscourt buy back the recovery step you owe. Running around for the inside-out forehand is the trap: it opens the whole deuce side while you are still moving backwards.
takeaway: Deep return, no +1 — reset crosscourt and earn the next ball.

scenario: Third set at 4-4. Your first-serve percentage has fallen from 60% to 35% since the second-set tiebreak, and your legs are gone even though the arm feels fine. First fix?
options: Take 10% off the pace and add spin
Keep the pace but aim well inside the lines
Keep the pace and go bigger to end points
explanation: Tired legs shorten the kinetic chain, so full pace flattens the trajectory and the ball clips the tape; less pace with spin restores the arc. Keeping the pace and aiming safer fails because your aim was never the problem.
takeaway: When the legs go, trade pace for arc.

scenario: Ad court, 40-30. Your kick second serve has been dying in the middle of the box all set, and the returner has stepped in and chipped two of them back to your feet.
options: Kick it deeper into the corner
Add more spin, same target
Flatten it out for more pace
explanation: A second serve that lands mid-box invites the returner forward, so the same kick aimed at the back corner pushes their contact back behind the baseline. More spin without depth is the classic fix that drops it even shorter.
takeaway: Second serve: same shape, deeper target.

scenario: 30-40, the first break point you've faced this set. Your opponent has stepped inside the baseline on five of your last six second serves and won three of those points.
options: First serve at 80%, spin, at the body
First serve flat down the T for the ace
First serve wide and follow it to the net
explanation: With the returner camped inside the baseline, the ball to avoid is a second serve, so an 80% spin first serve that jams the body is worth more than pace. Going flat for the T ace fails here — the miss hands them exactly what they want.
takeaway: On break point, make the first serve — the miss is the real risk.
mistakeType: going for too much on break point

scenario: Ad court, 30-15. The returner has set up a metre outside the singles sideline on every point this match, and your kick out wide keeps arriving where he is already standing.
options: Serve flat down the T
Kick wider, nearer the line
Serve heavy at his hip
explanation: Standing that wide leaves the whole T uncovered, and a flat serve there is the longest run you can ask him to make. Kicking wider only chases him into the ball he set his stance up to hit.
takeaway: Serve into the ground the returner has given away.

scenario: 5-3, serving for the set at 40-15. You've held every service game this set with the same wide-then-T pattern in the deuce court, and the returner still hasn't covered it.
options: Keep running the wide-then-T pattern
Switch to serves you haven't shown them yet
Serve everything at the body to stay safe
explanation: The pattern has held every game because the returner has not solved it, and the last game of a set is no time to test unproven targets. Switching to serves you haven't shown is tempting variety with no evidence behind it.
takeaway: Close the set with the pattern that built it.

scenario: 5-5, 30-30 against a 1.95 m opponent with an enormous wingspan. Both of your best wide serves this game came back deep with him barely leaving his spot on the baseline.
options: Serve into his front hip
Serve wider, closer to the line
Serve flat down the T line
explanation: Reach is what beats width, so a ball at the hip takes away the arm extension he returns with and cramps the swing. Serving wider is the instinct that fails here: it is the exact ball his wingspan handled twice already.
takeaway: You cannot stretch long arms — crowd them instead.

scenario: 30-30 in the deuce court, one point after a double fault. Your first serve has landed 65% all match; the fault came on a second serve you decelerated into.
options: Your normal first serve, full swing
Roll a 70% first serve in to be sure
Flatten it out and go for the ace
explanation: The evidence says your first serve is healthy and the fault came from deceleration, so a full normal swing is the lowest-risk ball available. Rolling in a 70% first serve is the tempting fix, but decelerating is what just failed you.
takeaway: After a double, swing fully at your normal first serve.

scenario: Second set, serving into a steady headwind on this end. Your kick second serves have been landing short and sitting up mid-box, and the returner has started stepping in on them.
options: Toss lower and in front, hit deeper
Add more spin and keep the same target
Toss higher and swing softer for control
explanation: A headwind brakes the ball and steals length, so a lower toss in front and a deeper, flatter target puts the serve back on the line. Adding more spin is the instinct that fails: it drops the serve even shorter into their strike zone.
takeaway: Into the wind: lower toss, deeper target.

scenario: 0-30 up on their serve, but they've just hit two 190 km/h first serves at your backhand and you're blocking from a metre behind the baseline. Where does this block go?
options: Deep down the middle, high over the net
Deep crosscourt into the open half
Low and short to drag them forward
explanation: Blocking from behind the baseline you can't control a sideline, and a deep middle ball takes away the server's angle while you recover. Deep crosscourt looks just as safe but leaks wide off a stretched block and opens the court.
takeaway: Stretched block: high, deep, down the middle.

focusTag: return position against a flat serve
scenario: 4-5 down, 30-30 on their serve. Their first serve is flat and around 150 km/h, and from a metre behind the baseline your deep blocks give them time to run around for the forehand.
options: Step up onto the baseline and take it earlier
Hold your spot and block deeper down the middle
Drop back another metre for reaction time
explanation: At 150 km/h with no kick you have time to meet the ball on the baseline, and earlier contact removes the setup time they keep using. Blocking deeper from a metre back is safe but leaves them the same free forehand.
takeaway: Take time away from a server who keeps getting set.

scenario: 4-4, 15-30 on their serve. On the last four second serves you waited to see the ball, decided somewhere around contact, and floated three returns short into the middle.
options: Pick your target before they toss
Pick it as the ball leaves the strings
Pick it once the ball has bounced
explanation: A target chosen before the toss lets the swing commit fully, which is exactly what those short floaters were missing. Deciding as the ball leaves the strings feels sharper but leaves you steering the racquet while the ball is on you.
takeaway: Choose the return target before they toss.

scenario: Deuce court, 30-30 on a fast, low-bouncing court. Their slice serve skids in below knee height to your forehand, and your last two topspin drives off it went into the net.
options: Slice it back low and deep
Drive it flat down the line
Roll heavy topspin crosscourt
explanation: Below the knee there is no height to lift from, so a slice travels with the skid and still lands deep with margin over the net. Rolling topspin off a ball at your shoelaces is what has already found the net twice.
takeaway: Low ball, low answer — slice it deep.

focusTag: split-step timing against a slow motion
scenario: Third set, 30-30. This server has a long, slow motion with a high toss, and you keep landing your split step and standing there flat-footed before the ball is even struck.
options: Delay the split to land at their contact
Keep splitting on your own usual rhythm
Split twice, once early and once late
explanation: The split only helps in the instant your feet reload, so against a slow motion it has to be delayed until their contact. Splitting twice looks like a fix, but the second hop lands late and freezes you as you need to push.
takeaway: Time the split to their contact, not your rhythm.

scenario: Their second serve kicks up at 140 km/h and you're 0-30 up on their serve. You've been returning from a metre behind the baseline and floating them back.
options: Move up and take it on the rise, crosscourt
Move up but go down the line for a winner
Stand back and block it safely
explanation: Moving up denies the kick its bounce height, and crosscourt gives you the longest court and the lowest net to set up the +1. Down the line off a rising kicking ball is the same aggression over the highest net with the least room.
takeaway: Attack a second serve by moving forward — and go crosscourt for margin.

scenario: You've just hit a deep crosscourt return to a righty's forehand in the deuce court, and they're stretched behind their own baseline. Where do you recover to before their contact?
options: A step to the crosscourt side
Straight back to the exact centre mark
Shade toward the down-the-line side
explanation: A stretched forehand from behind the baseline comes back crosscourt far more often than down the line, so bisecting their real angles means shading that way. Recovering to the exact centre mark is the default that ignores this ball.
takeaway: Recover to their likely reply, not to the centre mark.

scenario: 30-0 up on their serve. They are heavy-footed at the baseline, their second serve has been sitting up around 130 km/h, and they have netted two passing shots already this set.
options: Chip the return deep and follow it in
Drive the return deep and stay back
Block it deep and rally as usual
explanation: A cheap point at 30-0 is where you spend risk, and slow feet plus a sitting second serve plus two missed passes all point forward. Driving it and staying back is safer but hands them the baseline rally they are comfortable in.
takeaway: Spend the free point on the play that scares them.

scenario: Returning at 4-5, 30-30, you arrive at the return spot still holding your breath from the last rally. Where in the server's ritual does your exhale belong?
options: As they start bouncing the ball
As their racquet meets the ball
While you walk back to the line
explanation: Breathing out on the ball bounces releases tension while you still have time to load the split step, and it finishes before the toss needs your eyes. Exhaling at their contact is too late — you read and move on a held breath.
takeaway: Breathe out on their bounces, split on their contact.

scenario: 15-40 on their serve, two break points in hand. They've missed the first serve on six of the last eight points and the second sits up at 130 km/h.
options: Attack the first break point hardest
Play the first deep, attack only the second
Play both deep and make them win the points
explanation: The first break point is where the server is most likely to miss the first serve, so spend the aggression there instead of saving it. Playing the first deep and neutral hands back the very ball you earned the chance to attack.
takeaway: Spend the first break point, don't save it.

scenario: 2–2, neutral rally, both of you behind the baseline. She has carved three angle winners this set, each one off a ball you aimed near a corner. Nothing is open — where does this one go?
options: Deep through the middle, past her service line
Deep into the corner to move her again
A short angle to make her run forward
explanation: A deep middle ball hands her no angle to copy, so her reply has to come back through the centre where you already stand. Aiming at the corner again is what has fed her three winners: your angle becomes her angle.
takeaway: Against an angle player, the middle is a target.

scenario: 4–3 on a slow court. He plays from three metres behind his baseline and your last six heavy balls all came back with interest from back there. He has not stepped forward once.
options: A short crosscourt angle inside the box
A heavier, deeper ball to push him back further
A flat drive down the line to beat him
explanation: From three metres back he has eight extra metres to cover forward, and he has shown all match that he will not make that run. Hitting deeper only feeds the strength he built that court position for.
takeaway: If depth doesn't hurt them, pull them forward instead.

scenario: It's 4–4, deuce, and you've just dragged a heavy crosscourt forehand from well outside the deuce sideline. Your opponent takes it early and loves the down-the-line change. Where do you recover to?
options: A step ad-side of the centre mark
The centre mark, square to the middle
Stay wide and guard the line you left
explanation: Because your contact was outside the sideline, the two replies they can reach bisect on the ad side of centre, so a step past the mark covers both. The centre mark leaves you a stride late on anything into the ad court.
takeaway: Recover to the middle of their angles, not the middle of the court.

scenario: 3–3 against a left-hander. Your backhand crosscourt keeps landing on her forehand and she has drilled four of them for winners. This reply sits up short and central.
options: Drive it deep into her backhand corner
Trade crosscourt and out-steady her
Run around it for your forehand crosscourt
explanation: Against a left-hander the crosscourt diagonal you grew up trading feeds her forehand, and a short central ball is your chance to send it to the other corner instead. Running around it just reloads the same diagonal.
takeaway: Versus a lefty, check which corner holds the backhand.

scenario: Third set, 2–3, legs heavy. You're a metre behind the baseline and your last four forehands came off the frame, each one struck as the ball dropped past your hip.
options: Turn earlier, contact out in front
Back up a metre and let it drop
Step in and take it on the rise
explanation: Fatigue slows the feet, not the swing, so turning earlier restores a contact point in front where the frame stops appearing. Backing up feels safer but adds a step of running and drops contact even further behind you.
takeaway: Tired legs: turn earlier, don't reach later.
mistakeType: reaching for the ball when tired

scenario: 5–4, serving for the set. Your heavy crosscourt has pulled her wide and she is stretched and late on the ball for the third time this game. You are two metres behind your baseline.
options: Step up to the baseline as she stretches
Hold your ground and read the bounce
Drop back a step in case she goes deep
explanation: A stretched, late contact cannot produce depth, so the short reply is decided before she even hits it and the move belongs on her contact. Waiting to read the bounce is why you reached the last two of these late.
takeaway: Move on their contact, not on the bounce.

scenario: You've lost serve twice and you're making three unforced errors a game trying to finish rallies from the baseline. Your opponent retrieves everything from a metre behind hers.
options: Aim a metre higher, same pace
Swing harder and end points sooner
Take the pace off and just push
explanation: Raising net clearance a metre cuts errors without changing your game, because the same swing now lands deep instead of in the tape. Swinging harder against a retriever only shrinks the margin that is already failing you.
takeaway: Fix errors with height before you touch your pace.

scenario: 2–2, 30–15. Her crosscourt pulls you a step outside the sideline and you arrive in balance. She is back in the middle before you swing, and the line still looks tempting.
options: Send it back crosscourt, deep past her service line
Redirect it down the line into the open half
Drive it hard down the middle at her feet
explanation: From outside the sideline the line is the highest net, the shortest court and the longest recovery run for you. Crosscourt keeps the low net and the long diagonal — change direction from the middle of the court, not from its corner.
takeaway: Change direction from the middle, not from the corner.

scenario: 5–5 in the third and the rallies are running past ten balls. You're winning most of them, but you arrive at the ball gasping and your last two forehands sailed long from the middle of the baseline.
options: Breathe out at contact on every ball
Hold it, then breathe once the point ends
Take one deep breath before each serve
explanation: Exhaling on every contact keeps the core stable and stops the oxygen debt that turns long rallies into long errors. Holding it until the point ends is what most club players do, and it is exactly why the tenth ball flies.
takeaway: One exhale per contact, all rally long.

scenario: 3–4, 15–30. Her ball floats slow and flat with no kick and lands a metre inside your baseline. You have run around three of these and missed all three trying to end it.
options: Hit it back deep and wait for a shorter one
Back up and rip it flat for a winner
Take it early on the rise and go for the line
explanation: A ball landing a metre inside your baseline is deep, not short, and attacking from behind your own baseline is the shot that has already missed three times. Deep and heavy keeps the rally and buys the genuinely short one.
takeaway: Attack starts inside the baseline, not behind it.

focusTag: where to stop behind a short approach
scenario: 5–4, 30–30. Your approach lands short and they are already inside the baseline winding up, while you are still running and two steps short of the service line.
options: Stop where you are and split-step now
Keep sprinting to two metres from the net
Turn and recover behind the baseline
explanation: You cannot outrun their contact, and a split from a stopped position covers both passing lanes; arriving mid-stride covers neither. Sprinting the last two steps is what leaves you moving as the ball leaves their strings.
takeaway: Split where you are — never arrive mid-stride.

focusTag: recovering behind your own angle volley
scenario: 30–15. You cut a sharp crosscourt angle volley and they reach it, sliding wide past the doubles alley. You are still standing in the middle of the box where you volleyed from.
options: Shuffle across to the side you volleyed to
Close straight forward to the net tape
Hold the middle of the box and split
explanation: From out there their fastest reply is the line you left open, so moving across keeps you in front of it before they swing. Holding the centre feels balanced, but the ball is no longer in the centre and the geometry moved with it.
takeaway: Follow your volley across, not only forward.

focusTag: volley contact on the body ball
scenario: You closed behind an approach and they drive flat at your hip from the baseline. It's 30–30 and your last two body volleys were caught beside you and dumped into the net. Where's the contact?
options: Contact in front of your hip
Block it beside your body
Back up a step to make room
explanation: Contact in front of the lead hip keeps the racket face stable and sends the ball forward, which is how a body ball becomes an attacking volley. Blocking it beside your body gives the racket no room and drops it into the net.
takeaway: Meet body balls in front, never beside you.

scenario: You serve and volley at 30-30 and the return dips to your feet inside the service line. They have passed you twice down the line already this set.
options: Scoop it deep down the middle to buy time
Attempt a sharp angle volley winner
Let it bounce and play a groundstroke
explanation: A low first volley is a reset, and deep down the middle buys the step you need to reach proper volley position for the second one. The sharp angle winner from below net height is the shot that has to travel furthest over the highest net.
takeaway: First volleys at your feet are setups — not winners.
mistakeType: going for winners on low first volleys

focusTag: reading pass or lob from their contact
scenario: 4–4, 15–30. You are two metres in and your volley has pulled them into a full slide, contact below the knee behind the baseline. Their last two balls from there floated short.
options: Close two steps and cut it off
Drop back a step to cover the lob
Split where you are and let it drop
explanation: A contact below the knee on the run cannot be driven, so the reply floats and cutting it off early ends the point. Backing off for the lob is the right read when they are set with time, not when they are sliding.
takeaway: Low and sliding, close in; set and balanced, respect the lob.

focusTag: drop volley from the wrong distance
scenario: 40–30. A floater arrives at net height while you are still at the service line, and they are recovering behind their baseline after chasing your deep ball.
options: Punch it deep into the corner
Drop it short crosscourt over the net
Angle it sharply toward the sideline
explanation: From the service line the drop has seven metres to travel off a net-height contact, so it lands mid-court as a sitter. The drop is on two metres in with contact above the tape; from here depth is the shot.
takeaway: Service line: punch it deep. Net: drop it short.

focusTag: swing length on a hard pass
scenario: You poached and they answer with a hard flat pass at your chest from the service line. It's 30–40 and you've swung at the last two of these and flown both long.
options: Block it short and firm, no backswing
Take a full swing and try to end it
Soften the hands and slice it back
explanation: Their pace is already on the ball, so a short firm block redirects it and keeps the strings behind the shot. A full swing adds speed you do not need and is precisely what sent the last two long.
takeaway: Hard ball at you: block it, don't swing at it.

scenario: 3–3, 30–40. Following your approach in, their reply dips hard and lands at your feet just inside the service line. The two half-volleys you punched this set both flew long.
options: Block it soft and deep down the middle
Punch it hard and flat crosscourt
Stop, let it bounce, and lift it back
explanation: Their pace does the work, so a soft block deep through the middle clears the net and buys the step you need to close. Punching flat adds speed to a ball already carrying plenty, which is exactly why the last two sailed.
takeaway: Half-volley soft, deep and middle — never harder.

focusTag: overhead timing on a short lob
scenario: 40–30, you've closed to two metres from the net and they scramble up a floating lob dropping around your service line. There is no wind and the sun is behind you.
options: Cross-step back and take it in the air
Let it bounce first, then hit the overhead
Drop back and play it off the ground
explanation: A short floating lob in still air is a free smash, and taking it in the air keeps them scrambling instead of giving them two seconds back. Letting it bounce is right only on a deep heavy lob you cannot reach in balance.
takeaway: Short lob, hit it in the air; deep lob, let it bounce.

focusTag: volley target once they stop sprinting
scenario: 40–30. Your volley pushed them wide in the deuce corner, and by the time you meet the next one they have stopped, turned, and are jogging back toward the centre facing the middle.
options: Deep into the open ad court
Behind them into the deuce corner
Short and low down the middle
explanation: Their momentum is already carrying them to the centre, so the open ad corner is now the longest run and they arrive late or not at all. Hitting behind them only works while they are still at full sprint the other way.
takeaway: Still sprinting, hit behind. Turning back, open court.

focusTag: carrying a set into the next
scenario: You lost the first set 6–4 and three of those games ended with a double fault at deuce. You serve first in the second set against a returner standing two metres back.
options: Set one intention: full kick second serve to the backhand
Set a score goal: win the first three games of the set
Replay the double faults to find the toss problem
explanation: A lost set is only useful once it becomes one thing you will do, and a committed kick to the backhand attacks the exact game that broke you. The score goal of three games targets what you cannot control and rebuilds the same deuce tension.
takeaway: Turn a lost set into one thing you will do.

scenario: Serving at 30–30, your clean winner is called out and you saw the mark land in. Your opponent has already turned and is waiting to receive the next point.
options: Take the full time at the towel, then serve your usual pattern
Go straight back and serve flat and big while you are fired up
Play the next two points safe until the anger passes
explanation: The towel walk spends the adrenaline before it reaches your racquet and keeps your 30–30 serve pattern intact. Serving big while fired up feels like justice, but arousal that high shortens the swing and gives away the game instead.
takeaway: One bad call costs one point, not two.
mistakeType: playing angry after a bad call

scenario: Tiebreak at 3–4 and you have just missed the first serve. Both of your double faults today came on second serves you flattened out under pressure.
options: Hit your normal kick second serve to the backhand
Push it in softly and start the rally from behind
Flatten it out so the return cannot be attacked
explanation: Breakers are decided by the points you hand over, and your practised kick neither double faults nor invites a free swing. Pushing it in softly avoids the fault but donates the mini-break on the return one shot later.
takeaway: In a breaker, serve the second serve you practise.

scenario: Break point down at 30–40, you step in on a mid-court forehand. Your last two forehands from that spot flew long and the words in your head are ‘don’t miss’.
options: Pick a target: crosscourt, two metres inside the baseline
Cue the technique: finish the swing over your shoulder
Take the pace off and roll it deep to the middle
explanation: An external target gives attention one job and lets a rehearsed swing run itself on the shot you just missed twice. The technique cue turns the stroke into a thought under pressure, which is what sent those two forehands long.
takeaway: Aim at a spot, not at your swing.

scenario: Your opponent bounces once and serves within eight seconds, and you have lost three straight return games playing at that speed. You are 1–4 down, walking in to receive.
options: Stay at the back fence and take your own full time
Match their tempo to keep them from settling in
Return from a step further back to buy yourself time
explanation: The receiver decides when play starts, so taking your full time rebuilds the routine you have gone three return games without. Matching their tempo keeps you inside their rhythm and leaves you choosing a return target after the toss.
takeaway: The receiver owns the clock — use it.

scenario: Your opponent has won four games in a row, jogs between points and serves within ten seconds. You are 2–5 down and about to serve.
options: Use your full time between points and towel at the change
Start the game quickly before they settle into it
Switch to a different style for a couple of games
explanation: A streak runs on tempo, and taking your full time leaves them standing still with a lead to think about. Starting quickly to catch them cold keeps the match at the speed that just produced four straight games.
takeaway: Cool a hot streak by slowing the clock.

scenario: You were broken serving for the match at 5–4 and they now serve at 5–5. They have missed the first serve on six of the last eight points.
options: Step in on their second serve early in the game
Extend the rallies and let the pressure work on them
Go big on the first return to break straight back
explanation: They are serving their tightest game of the match, so standing in on that second serve converts their dropping first-serve rate into pressure immediately. Extending rallies gives them time to settle and hands back the discomfort.
takeaway: They serve scared too — stand in and take it.

scenario: You have lost five of the last six games. The one thing still working is the kick serve to the ad-court backhand: eight of nine points won behind it today.
options: Start every service point with that kick serve
Serve and volley to shorten the points instead
Grind long rallies until the ball feels clean
explanation: Confidence comes back from points won, and the serve already producing eight of nine is the cheapest source of them. Serving and volleying to shorten points adds an unrehearsed skill at the moment your margin is smallest.
takeaway: Lean on what is already winning points.

scenario: You lost 6–4, 6–4 to a player you had beaten twice before. Driving home, you can still see the three volleys you missed at 4–4 in the second set.
options: Write two things that worked and one fix, tonight
List every error you made while it is still fresh
Head to the practice court tomorrow and drill volleys
explanation: Two-plus-one keeps the review short enough to stay accurate and leaves practice with one clear job. Listing every error while it is fresh is rumination with a notebook, and it teaches your memory that the match was only misses.
takeaway: Two things that worked, one to fix — then stop.

scenario: First time against this opponent and five minutes of warm-up remain. You have rallied from the baseline but have not yet seen their backhand or their second serve.
options: Feed a few balls to each wing and watch which one floats
Groove your own forehand until the contact feels clean
Hit at half pace and save your legs for the match
explanation: The warm-up is the only free scouting you get, and knowing which wing floats decides your first three service patterns. Grooving your own forehand feels productive but walks you to the first point with no plan for where the ball goes.
takeaway: Warm up your plan, not only your strokes.

scenario: You and your partner are one-up-one-back. Your baseline partner gets a short, floaty ball mid-court. What should you both do?
options: Both move up to the net together behind the approach
Stay put — keep one player back to cover
Partner hits it and retreats to the baseline
explanation: A short ball is your cue to get BOTH players to the net. The both-up formation wins the majority of club points, so your partner approaches and joins you.
takeaway: Short ball = both up. The team that reaches the net first usually wins the point.
scenarioTr: Sen ve partnerin biri-önde-biri-arkada dizilimindesiniz. Arkadaki partnerin kısa, yumuşak bir top alıyor. İkiniz ne yapmalısınız?
optionsTr: İkiniz birlikte file'ye çıkın (yaklaşma vuruşunun arkasından)
Olduğunuz yerde kalın — biriniz arkada kalsın
explanationTr: Kısa top, ikinizi de file'ye çıkarma işaretidir. Her ikisi de file'de (both-up) dizilimi kulüp puanlarının çoğunu kazanır; partnerin yaklaşıp sana katılır.
takeawayTr: Kısa top = ikiniz de file'ye. File'ye önce ulaşan takım genelde puanı alır.
scenarioFr: Ton partenaire et toi êtes un devant, un derrière. Ton partenaire de fond récupère une balle courte et flottante au milieu du court. Que faites-vous ?
optionsFr: Monter tous les deux au filet derrière l'approche
Ne rien changer — garder un joueur derrière pour couvrir
Il frappe et retourne à la ligne de fond
explanationFr: Une balle courte, c'est le signal pour amener les DEUX joueurs au filet. La formation deux-devant gagne la majorité des points en club : ton partenaire monte et te rejoint.
takeawayFr: Balle courte = les deux devant. L'équipe qui arrive au filet la première gagne généralement le point.

scenario: Your partner is returning at 30–40 on their serve and you are the returner's partner. The opposing net player has already picked off two returns for winners this game.
options: Service line, eyes on the net player
Back on the baseline beside your partner
Tight to the net, ready to volley
explanation: From the service line you can step in on a good return or turn and run down a lob, and watching the volleyer tells your team what is coming before the ball does. Standing on the baseline concedes the net to a team that already owns it.
takeaway: Returner's partner: service line, eyes on the volleyer.
mistakeType: net player glued to the alley

scenario: You serve and volley at 30-30, and the return dips LOW at your feet just inside the service line. Both opponents are already at the net.
options: Deep to the baseline returner
Hard at the opposing net player
A soft drop into their service box
explanation: From below net height you must lift, so the deep ball to the baseliner is the only target that does not arrive as a sitter. Hard at the net player is the reflex, and a lifted volley there is the easiest put-away in doubles.
takeaway: First-volley target depends on height: a low ball goes deep/middle, not at the net player.
mistakeType: first volley auto-aimed at the net player

scenario: You're returning serve in doubles against a team with one player at the net. What's the priority on your return?
options: Keep it LOW, cross-court at the volleyer's feet
Drive it deep and flat down the middle
Loop it high cross-court for safety
explanation: A low cross-court return at the incoming volleyer's feet is the hardest ball to attack. A floaty/high return is poach bait. Your goal is to get your team forward, not to win it outright.
takeaway: Doubles return = low at the volleyer's feet. Floaters get poached.
scenarioTr: Biri file'de olan bir takıma karşı çiftlerde karşılama yapıyorsun. Karşılamada öncelik ne?
optionsTr: ALÇAK tut, çaprazda voleyi yapanın ayaklarına
Güvenli olsun diye yükseğe, çaprazda lob gibi
explanationTr: Voleye gelenin ayaklarına alçak çapraz karşılama, saldırması en zor toptur. Yüksek/yumuşak karşılama poach yemidir. Amaç puanı tek vuruşta bitirmek değil, takımını öne taşımak.
takeawayTr: Çiftlerde karşılama = voleyi yapanın ayaklarına alçak. Yumuşak toplar poach yer.
scenarioFr: Tu retournes en double contre une équipe avec un joueur au filet. Quelle est la priorité sur ton retour ?
optionsFr: Le garder BAS, croisé, dans les pieds du volleyeur
Le frapper profond et à plat au milieu
Le lifter haut en croisé, par sécurité
explanationFr: Un retour bas et croisé dans les pieds du volleyeur qui monte est la balle la plus difficile à attaquer. Un retour haut et flottant se fait intercepter. Ton but est de faire avancer ton équipe, pas de gagner le point d'un coup.
takeawayFr: Retour en double = bas, dans les pieds du volleyeur. Les balles flottantes se font intercepter.

scenario: You're the net player at 30-30 and you've decided to poach this point. Your partner is serving to the body and the returner has blocked every one crosscourt.
options: Just after the serve bounces
The instant your partner tosses
Once the return clears the net
explanation: Crossing as the serve bounces is early enough to cut off the middle and late enough that the returner can no longer redirect behind you. Moving on the toss shows your hand while they can still change the target.
takeaway: Poach as the returner starts the swing — not too early, not too late.

scenario: Their lob drops as you back up to the service line and both of them retreat to the baseline. You have already dumped two smashes into the net today going for the alley.
options: Deep down the middle, then close in
Sharply angled into their open alley
Short and soft into the open court
explanation: From the service line the angle needs a metre of net height you do not have, while a deep middle smash splits two retreating players and leaves you an easy volley to finish. The alley smash is the one already in the net twice.
takeaway: Angle smashes from close in, middle smashes from deep.

scenario: 4–4 on their serve. Their net player has floated six volleys this set, while the server is solid off both wings. Your partner asks where the big points should go.
options: Keep the ball on the weaker volleyer's racket
Play the middle and split the two of them
Attack the sidelines to make them both run
explanation: Six floated volleys in a set is a rate, not an accident, so the points that decide the match belong to the racket most likely to hand them back. The middle ball is safe but lets whichever of them is more comfortable take it.
takeaway: Big points go at the weaker racket.
mistakeType: serve placement that doesn't set up the partner

focusTag: attacking two players at the net
scenario: 5–4 down, both of you back and both opponents at the net — but they are standing on their service line, not tight to it. Your ball arrives at waist height.
options: Low through the middle at their feet
A lob over the closer one's shoulder
Hard down the alley past the closer one
explanation: Standing off the net they must volley up from below the tape, and the middle ball leaves them the smallest angle plus a moment of hesitation. The lob answers a team crowding the net; against this one it is a free overhead.
takeaway: Tight to the net, lob them; off the net, go low and middle.

scenario: A big server is crushing your partner's return and picking off your net player. What formation adjustment helps?
options: Both go back for a game, then work forward again
Keep one up and shorten your partner's return swing
Both move up to take the return early
explanation: Both-back absorbs a serve your partner cannot block from a normal return position, and it is temporary — you climb back once a return lands deep. Keeping one up only asks the same net player to survive the same ball again.
takeaway: Both-back is a shield you raise, not a formation you live in.
mistakeType: leaving the net player exposed to a big serve

scenario: Their net player has poached four of your last six returns, standing a step off the centre line. You're returning at 30-30 in the deuce court.
options: Lob the crowding net player
Hit harder through the same spot
Aim your return down their alley
explanation: A lob over a crowding poacher wins the point outright or pushes them back for the rest of the game, which is the real prize. Hitting harder through the same spot is exactly the ball they are standing there to intercept.
takeaway: Punish an over-eager poacher with a lob — it buys back the middle.

scenario: Deuce court, 30-30. You've noticed the returner chips a short, floaty backhand every time you serve into their body. What's the highest-value play?
options: Body again, then attack the chip
Go for a flat ace down the T
Serve wide to open the court
explanation: You've read a reliable tendency. The body serve jams the backhand and forces the short floater — so trigger it on purpose, anticipate the reply, move in, and attack it on the rise. You're hunting the +1, not the ace.
takeaway: When you've read a return tendency, serve to trigger it — then pounce on the predictable reply.
mistakeType: ignoring a read for a low-percentage ace

scenario: 4-5 down, 0-30 on the return, fast court, against a big server who goes 70% to your backhand. Where do you stand and what's the goal?
options: Shade to the backhand, block deep middle
Hold your spot and rip a clean winner
Back up two metres and slice it
explanation: Against a bomb on a fast court the realistic goal is a neutral return, not a winner. Shade toward the 70% target, shorten to a block, and aim deep down the middle — it cuts the server's next angle and buys time to recover.
takeaway: Vs a big server: shade to the pattern, block deep middle, accept neutral — survive before you attack.
mistakeType: going for a winner off an unreturnable serve

scenario: A long crosscourt forehand exchange, both deep. Your opponent's crosscourt is landing a little shorter each ball. What's the highest-percentage way to change the pattern?
options: Wait for the short one, then change direction
Rip it down the line off a deep ball
Keep grinding the same crosscourt
explanation: The shortening ball is your cue: step in on that one and change direction down the line into their backhand. Changing direction off a deep ball is the low-percentage version of the same idea, and it is the one that misses.
takeaway: Change direction off the short ball, not the deep one.
mistakeType: changing direction off a deep defensive ball

scenario: You approached down the line and you're at the service line — not yet at the net — as your opponent loads up for a crosscourt pass. What's the play?
options: Split, cover crosscourt, punch it deep
Sprint to the net and guess a side
Retreat to the baseline for the pass
explanation: From the service line you can't angle a volley safely. Your DTL approach already closed the line, so split-step, cover the higher-percentage crosscourt pass, and punch the volley DEEP behind the moving opponent — depth over a risky angle from too far back.
takeaway: Caught at the service line: split, cover the crosscourt, volley deep behind them — not a fancy angle.
mistakeType: attempting an angled volley from too far back

scenario: You served for the set at 5-3 and got broken to 5-4 after two double faults. What's the reset for the next game?
options: Slow the routine, widen the target
Go for broke to win the break back
Replay the faults to fix the toss
explanation: After a choke-break the fix is process, not panic. Slow your tempo between points, breathe, and reset to a bigger target (margin over the lines). Don't chase the break back recklessly or ruminate on the misses — play the next point on its own merits.
takeaway: After a choke: slow the tempo, widen your margins, play the next point — don't chase or ruminate.
mistakeType: panicking or ruminating after a costly game

scenario: You're serving in doubles, partner at the net. The returner has burned your partner twice with crosscourt returns dipping at their feet. Best adjustment?
options: Switch to I-formation or fake a poach
Have your partner back off a step
Just serve harder up the T
explanation: The returner has a comfortable, grooved target — crosscourt at the net player's feet. Take it away by hiding where the net player will be: I-formation or a fake poach forces the returner to decide late and abandon a pattern that's been working.
takeaway: When a returner grooves a target, hide your net player — I-formation or a fake resets their decision.
mistakeType: staying predictable against a hot returner

focusTag: serving to set up your weapon
scenario: Ad court, 30-15, and you're a righty whose forehand is the weapon. You've served wide six times this game and five returns have come back deep to your backhand corner.
options: Serve T to force the return middle
Serve at the body to cramp their swing
Serve wide again with even more pace
explanation: A T serve takes the returner's angle away, so the reply comes back centrally — the one ball you can run around and load the forehand on. Serving wide again keeps working the door that has sent five straight returns to your backhand.
takeaway: Serve where the return feeds your best shot.

scenario: Break point down at 30-40 in the ad court. Your second serve has been landing short all day, and the righty returner has run around every ball he can reach to hit a forehand.
options: Heavy kick at the body to jam them
Kick out wide to their backhand corner
Flat second serve down the T line
explanation: A body serve leaves a run-around returner no room to open up, and the kick gives net clearance when your arm is tight. Kicking wide to the backhand is textbook, but here it hands him the step-around forehand he has hunted all match.
takeaway: Tight arm, big point: kick into the body.

focusTag: serving against a deep return position
scenario: Deuce court, 40-15 on a slow hard court. The returner has stood two metres behind the baseline all match and blocked your biggest first serves back deep down the middle.
options: Slice wide into the deuce corner
Same target, ten km/h more pace
Heavy kick high to the backhand
explanation: Standing that deep buys him time against pace but leaves him a long way from the sideline, so width drags him wider still and opens the court for your next ball. More pace at the same spot is the serve he has been blocking back all match.
takeaway: Against a deep returner add width, not speed.
mistakeType: answering depth with pace instead of angle

scenario: You're a lefty serving at 30-40 in the ad court. The righty returner stands well inside the sideline, and he has already hurt you twice today off your T serve.
options: Slice wide, dragging the backhand off court
Heavy kick at the body, then take the middle
Flat down the T again for the ace
explanation: Standing inside the sideline gives your lefty slice its whole runway, and the ball curves further from the backhand the wider it lands. Going back down the T is the tempting variation, but that is the serve he has punished twice.
takeaway: Lefty, ad court, big point: slice it wide.
mistakeType: wasting the lefty advantage on big points

scenario: Serving for the set at 5-4, 40-30 in the ad court. Your flat T attempts have landed one of seven this set, and you have won eight of nine points behind a first serve that went in.
options: Kick wide at three-quarter pace
Flat down the T for the ace
Soft spin into the middle of the box
explanation: A made first serve is worth far more than a fast one, and three-quarter kick keeps that advantage without the miss rate of a one-in-seven target. Pushing a soft serve into the middle is the other trap on set point.
takeaway: Big point: make the first serve, keep the spin.
mistakeType: donating big points with hero serves

scenario: Ad court, 15-30, and you have missed the first serve. The one-hander across the net drove two of your low slice serves for winners today, but chips anything above shoulder height back short.
options: Kick it up to the backhand shoulder
Slice it low and wide to the backhand
Kick it heavy into the body
explanation: The evidence says height, not width, breaks this backhand, and a kick climbing above the shoulder buys you the short chip to attack. Slicing low and wide feeds the strike zone that has already produced two winners.
takeaway: One-hander struggling high? Serve up, not wide.
mistakeType: serving low to a player who loves low balls

scenario: Ad court, 40-0. Your kick out wide has produced two aces this game, and on the second one the returner never moved his feet, framing it late from exactly the same spot.
options: Serve the same kick out wide
Switch to the flat T for surprise
Serve at the body to vary it
explanation: Nothing in his feet has changed, so the serve is still free money; you change the pattern when the returner adjusts, not when repeating it starts to feel uncomfortable. Switching to the T gives back a point the wide serve was winning.
takeaway: Keep serving it until they move.

scenario: 30-30, with two double faults already this game. Watching yourself, you're starting the motion within a second of stepping to the line, before your breathing has settled at all.
options: Bounce, breathe, serve to a spin target
Serve straight away before the doubt builds
Use the full time allowed each point
explanation: A short deliberate reset lets the breathing catch up and gives the swing a spin target to commit to, which is what a rushed motion lacks. Serving straight away to outrun the doubt keeps the shortened motion that produced both faults.
takeaway: Reset the ritual, then commit to a spin target.

scenario: Deuce court, 30-30, against a left-hander. Your first serves down the T have come back as three forehand winners today, all struck from inside the baseline.
options: Slice it wide to the deuce corner
Flat down the T again, harder
Serve at the body to jam him
explanation: Against a left-hander the deuce-court T runs straight into the forehand, which is where those three winners came from, while the slice curves away to the backhand. Hitting the same T harder just speeds up his favourite ball.
takeaway: Lefty in the deuce court: wide finds the backhand.

scenario: Second set with a strong wind at your back on this end. Three of your flat first serves have flown a foot long already and you're serving at 15-30.
options: Add spin and aim shorter in the box
Keep the target, take pace off the serve
Keep it flat and aim right at the line
explanation: A tailwind adds length, so topspin brings the ball down earlier and a shorter target keeps your margin inside the service line. Just taking pace off is the common fix, but a slow flat serve still rides the wind long.
takeaway: Wind behind you: more spin, shorter target.

scenario: Deuce court, 40-15. Your wide serve drags the returner two steps outside the alley, and the block return floats back crosscourt, landing short of your service line.
options: Forehand into the open ad court, deep
Forehand behind them to the deuce corner
Forehand deep up the middle, then move in
explanation: They are still outside the alley and the short floater gives you time, so the open ad court is the biggest target available. Hitting behind them wrong-foots, but that only pays once they start sprinting early to recover.
takeaway: Wide serve, short reply — hit the space, not the body.
mistakeType: overcomplicating the +1 with the court open

scenario: Break point down at 30-40, second serve. The toss drifts a foot behind your head as it leaves your hand, the same drift that sent both of your last first serves long.
options: Let it drop and start again
Arch back and hit it anyway
Shorten the swing and steer it
explanation: Letting a toss fall untouched costs you nothing but a few seconds, and that drift behind your head is exactly what has been sending serves long. Arching back to reach it is the brave-looking choice that bakes the fault into the swing.
takeaway: Do not serve a toss you do not trust.

scenario: Your opponent has chipped fourteen of sixteen returns, all landing short of your service line and below net height. You're serving at 30-30 on a medium-paced hard court.
options: Move in as you land from the serve
Wait for the chip to bounce, then move in
Hold the baseline and rally from there
explanation: Fourteen short chips is a pattern you can move on before the ball lands, and taking it above net height turns their reply into your approach. Waiting for the bounce feels safer, but the ball is dying and you arrive to a low volley.
takeaway: Against a chipper, move in off your own landing.

scenario: 15-40 down, serving in the deuce court. Your wide slice has landed eight of ten today and drawn short returns, while the flat T you keep reaching for is two of nine.
options: Wide slice on both points
Flat T on the first point
Take pace off and roll both in
explanation: Two break points down is precisely when you play your best percentage, and a serve landing eight of ten with a weak reply is worth running twice. The flat T feels braver but at two of nine it is a donated break.
takeaway: Break points down: run your highest-percentage serve.
mistakeType: serving away from an attacking returner

scenario: Serving from the west end at 3-3, the low sun sits exactly in your toss line. You've missed four of five first serves from this end and made every one from the other.
options: Angle the toss out of the glare
Shift a step along the baseline, same serve
Keep the toss and serve on feel, eyes down
explanation: Angling the toss out of the sun and accepting a spin-first serve keeps your eyes on the ball, the only variable that decides this point. Sliding a step along the baseline rarely helps — a low sun travels with you down the line.
takeaway: Move the toss out of the sun before the score forces you.
mistakeType: refusing to adapt the toss to conditions

scenario: Deuce court, 30-30, a 150 km/h first serve into your forehand that you meet balanced on the baseline. Their backhand has leaked three short balls this set, and from here it sits down the line.
options: Deep crosscourt with margin
Down the line to the backhand
Deep up the middle to stay neutral
explanation: Crosscourt gives you the longest court and the lowest net, which is what a return needs before it needs a target. Going down the line to hunt the weak backhand asks for the highest net and the shortest court off a 150 km/h serve.
takeaway: Buy margin on the return; buy the weakness on the next ball.

scenario: Ad court, 15-30 up. Their second serve keeps sitting up short, and you have missed four of six returns going for the finish from your usual spot a metre behind the baseline.
options: Step a metre in, same swing speed
Stay back and swing harder at it
Stay back and roll it deep instead
explanation: The extra pressure on a short second serve comes from meeting it earlier, so move the feet up and keep the swing you trust. Swinging harder from deep is what has put four of six returns into the net and the back fence.
takeaway: Attack a second serve with your feet, not your arm.
mistakeType: standing deep against weak second serves

scenario: Deuce court, 0-30 down on a fast indoor hard court. Their flat first serve has produced four late, framed returns off your backhand in the last two games.
options: Shorten to a block, contact in front
Keep the full swing but start it earlier
Step back a metre and swing normally
explanation: Framed returns mean the racquet is late, and a compact block gets contact in front while borrowing the server's pace. Keeping the full swing and starting earlier sounds like the fix, but a long backswing is what you can't start in time.
takeaway: Late on the return? Cut the swing, not the reaction.

scenario: Break point for you at 30-40. Their second serve has gone to your backhand on nine of eleven points this set, and it lands short of the service line.
options: Run around it for the forehand
Wait, react, keep options open
Chip it back safely and rally
explanation: On a serve this predictable the returner who has already decided wins the exchange, and the run-around forehand is the shot that punishes a short second serve. Waiting to react turns a known ball into an ordinary one.
takeaway: On break points, return with a decision, not a reaction.

scenario: Ad court, 15-30 up. Their kick keeps climbing above your backhand shoulder, and every time you back up to take it falling they step inside the baseline and own the middle.
options: Step in and meet it before the peak
Back up further and take it falling
Stand still and swing over the high ball
explanation: Meeting the kick before it peaks turns a shoulder-high ball into a waist-high one and keeps the return deep enough to hold them back. Backing up further is more comfortable but gives them the step forward they have used all game.
takeaway: Beat the kick with your feet, before the bounce peaks.

scenario: They have served and volleyed on both break points this set and are coming in again at 30-40. Their first volley is struck from around the service line.
options: Low at their feet as they close
A high deep lob over them
The hardest drive you have
explanation: Contact below net height mid-run forces a defensive half-volley you can attack on the next ball. The lob is the other real answer, but from a return you rarely have the time to place it well enough.
takeaway: Against the rusher: make their first volley come from their shoelaces.

scenario: 0-3 down in the set. In every one of their service games you have missed the first two returns going for too much, and only started making balls once the game was already gone.
options: Make the first two returns deep and neutral
Go for winners early while the game is open
Change your return position on every point
explanation: Two made returns puts you at 15-15 with the server still working, and pressure in a return game comes from being level, not from early winners. Going big on the first two points is what has handed over a free 30-0 all set.
takeaway: Win return games by starting them level.
mistakeType: even effort distribution across return games

scenario: 5-5, 30-30 on their serve. Your last six returns have all landed inside their service line, and they have stepped in and hit four forehand winners off those short balls.
options: Aim two metres higher over the net
Swing harder to push the ball deeper
Aim closer to the sidelines to move them
explanation: Depth is bought with net clearance, so lifting the target a couple of metres above the tape moves the bounce back towards their baseline. Swinging harder is the usual answer and it fails: a flatter ball still lands short, only sooner.
takeaway: Returns go deep because they fly higher, not faster.
mistakeType: missing the split step on return

scenario: Third set on their serve. Across five service games their toss has drifted a foot to their right before every slice, and stayed over the head for the kick. How do you use it?
options: Lean that way as their racquet drops
Commit to the side as the toss leaves the hand
Wait for the bounce, then chase it down
explanation: Leaning at the racquet drop uses the read but still leaves you time to stop if this one is different, which is the point of a half-step. Committing at the toss is the greedy version — a server who sees the lean serves the other way.
takeaway: Use the tell late: lean at the racquet drop, not the toss.

scenario: You hit a deep return, watch it land, and their reply passes you down the line. Replaying it, you were still standing where you returned from when they made contact.
options: Move as you finish the follow-through
Move once the return lands on their side
Move when you read their swing direction
explanation: Recovery starts on your own follow-through because it is the only free time in the exchange, and by their contact you must already be split and centred. Waiting for the ball to land leaves you two steps short of any ball hit on the rise.
takeaway: Start recovering on your follow-through, not on their bounce.

focusTag: when the line return is on
scenario: Deuce court, 40-15. Their second serve sits up short, you step in and take it at hip height, and the server has already drifted a step towards the deuce sideline to cover the crosscourt.
options: Drive it down the line behind them
Drive it crosscourt into the corner
Roll it deep up the middle and rally
explanation: A short serve met early inside the baseline is the one ball that pays for the higher net down the line, and they have already committed the other way. Crosscourt is the safer shape but lands where they are standing.
takeaway: Earn the line with a short ball and early contact.

scenario: Deuce court, 30-30. They have jammed three serves straight into your hip this game, and both times you tried to turn a forehand out of it the return sat up short mid-court.
options: Step out of the ball's line, block backhand
Rotate the hips and squeeze a forehand
Lean back and block it from the chest
explanation: A body serve is a space problem, and one hard step clear of the ball's line gives the compact backhand block the room the forehand never gets. Squeezing the forehand out is what produced two short balls already.
takeaway: Body serve: move your feet clear, block backhand.

scenario: Ad court at 30-15, their righty slice serve pulls you a step outside the sideline. You reach it balanced but stretched, and they have stayed back.
options: High and deep crosscourt
Flat down the line on the stretch
A sharp short angle back
explanation: Stretched wide you need height for safety and depth for time, and crosscourt is the longest path while you recover the court you just left. Flat down the line on the stretch is the lowest-margin ball available from that position.
takeaway: Stretched = high, deep, crosscourt. Save the line for balance.
mistakeType: changing direction off a deep defensive ball

scenario: Two sets in against the same server. You've stood in the same spot on every return, and they've hit the same wide slice on eleven of their last twelve first serves.
options: Move your starting depth around between points
Stand a metre further back for the rest of the set
Keep your spot and read the toss instead
explanation: Eleven of twelve to one target means they are aiming off a fixed reference, so changing your depth point to point forces a fresh aim every time. Moving back once only gives them a new fixed target to groove against within a game.
takeaway: Keep moving the target they're aiming at.

scenario: You've missed three first-serve returns in a row against a 190 km/h serve and you're 0-40 down. Their two second serves this set both landed at around 140 km/h.
options: Land first returns, attack the seconds
Attack each serve until one finally lands
Chip returns back and start the rally
explanation: Against a 190 km/h serve a return that simply lands deep is already a win, and the 140 km/h second serves are where break points are actually built. Attacking each serve until one lands feels brave, but it donates points you cannot afford at 0-40.
takeaway: Survive the first serve, hunt the second.

focusTag: adapting to a slow, high-bouncing court
scenario: First match of the clay season, 2–3 down. The flat drives that win for you on hard courts are coming back easily, and four of them have landed long by half a metre.
options: Add topspin and hit with more net clearance
Hit flatter and earlier to beat the slow bounce
Take pace off and keep everything short and safe
explanation: Clay slows the ball and lifts the bounce, so the flat drive that lands deep on a hard court sails long here while spin brings it down and pushes her back. Hitting flatter and earlier fights the surface instead of using it.
takeaway: On slow courts, buy depth with spin, not speed.

scenario: 30–30 on your serve in a neutral crosscourt rally. Your opponent stands right on the baseline, takes everything early, and every flat ball you hit comes back faster than you sent it.
options: Add height and land it deeper
Flatten out and hit through them harder
Go for a short angle to drag them in
explanation: A deep, heavy ball pushes an early-taking opponent behind the baseline and steals the timing their whole game runs on. Hitting through them harder is the tempting reply, but pace into their strike zone is what they redirect.
takeaway: Beat an early taker with depth, not speed.

scenario: 40–30. Your forehand into the deuce corner has him at full sprint across the baseline, and he is still accelerating away from you as the reply reaches your racket. The ad court is empty.
options: Behind him, back into the deuce corner
Into the empty ad court he is sprinting toward
Deep down the middle to reset the point
explanation: While he is still accelerating across, reversing costs him two steps he does not have, so the ball behind him is unreachable. The empty court is the right answer only once he has stopped and started back toward the middle.
takeaway: Behind them while they run; open court once they turn.
mistakeType: always hitting to the open court

scenario: At 3-4, 30-30 they pull you two metres behind the baseline and you barely reach the ball. They are balanced on their own baseline, waiting.
options: High and deep down the middle
A flat counter-winner attempt
A drop shot from behind the baseline
explanation: Height is time: a high deep middle ball lands far from both corners and gives you the seconds to rebuild court position. The flat counter-winner from that far back has almost no margin and ends the point for them.
takeaway: In trouble, buy time with height — not risk with pace.

scenario: Third set, 3–3. You hold serve comfortably on two- and three-shot points, but in return games you are 1 for 9 going for a winner by the fourth ball.
options: Play the return games longer and take fewer risks
Attack her second serve harder for a quick break
Play every game exactly the same way for rhythm
explanation: Your serve already shortens points for you, so the break has to come from the rally length she likes least: one more ball, not one bigger swing. Attacking harder is what produced eight of those nine errors.
takeaway: Short points on your serve, long ones on hers.
mistakeType: resetting instead of attacking short balls

scenario: Your inside-out forehand is your best shot and you've hit two winners with it. It's 4-4, 30-30, and you're in a neutral rally from the middle of the baseline.
options: A deep ball to their backhand
Any ball down the middle
Short angles to their forehand
explanation: Pressure their backhand deep and the usual reply is a slower crosscourt into your backhand corner, which is exactly the ball you can run around. A ball down the middle gives them no reason to send it anywhere in particular.
takeaway: Your forehand hunt starts two shots earlier, on their backhand.
mistakeType: waiting for weapons instead of building them

scenario: 4–5, 30–40 and a set point against you. You're in a neutral forehand exchange from the deuce corner, both of you behind the baseline, and nothing on their side is open yet.
options: Go crosscourt again, over the low middle
Change direction down the line
Drive it flat up the middle at them
explanation: With nothing open, crosscourt buys the lowest net, the longest court and the shortest recovery, three margins for free on a set point. Changing direction down the line off a deep ball asks for the highest net and the shortest court.
takeaway: On big points, choose the direction with the most margin.

scenario: 5–5, 30–30. Her drop shot pulls you up to the service line and you reach it low but on balance. She has stayed back on her own baseline to watch.
options: Deep down the line, the way you're facing
A soft drop shot back over the net
Deep crosscourt into the far corner
explanation: From the service line the line ball is the shortest flight, so it lands before she can cover it and you keep the forecourt position her drop shot handed you. Crosscourt travels farthest and gives her time to pass you.
takeaway: Answer a drop shot down the line, then hold your ground.

scenario: They redirect everything you hit hard and have won six of the last eight rallies. It's 2-4 and their contact point is always waist high, on the baseline.
options: High, heavy loops above the shoulder
More pace to try to out-hit them
Stand closer in and take it early
explanation: A slow ball above shoulder height makes a pace-lover generate their own power, which is where their timing and patience break. Adding pace is the instinct and it feeds the exact ball they have been redirecting all set.
takeaway: Starve the counter-puncher: no pace to borrow.

scenario: You crack a short sharp crosscourt angle from the deuce side and they only just reach it, stretched wide outside the alley. You're still standing a metre inside the baseline after the shot.
options: Follow it in and close the net
Recover to the centre mark as usual
Hold deep behind the baseline and reset
explanation: Pulling them that wide also handed them a counter-angle, and from a metre inside the baseline the only way to cover it is forward. Recovering to the centre mark leaves the short angle you just opened completely free.
takeaway: Insure every angle you hit by closing behind it.
mistakeType: admiring an angle instead of closing

scenario: Serving at 4–5, 30–30. Their heavy topspin keeps kicking above your backhand shoulder, and your last three replies floated short from a metre behind the baseline.
options: Back up a step and take it later
Stand in and take it early on the rise
Drive it flat at shoulder height
explanation: One step back lets the kick drop into your strike zone, where the same backhand goes deep instead of floating short. Taking it on the rise is the brave answer, but a rising kick above the shoulder is the hardest contact you own.
takeaway: Give a kicking ball one step and it becomes a normal ball.
mistakeType: recovering to the hash instead of the bisector

scenario: 2–2 in the first, backhand to backhand crosscourt, both steady. Your backhand is the weaker wing and you've missed two of the last five, while they take it early from on the baseline.
options: Loop it higher and heavier crosscourt
Rip it down the line to their forehand
Flatten out and take it earlier
explanation: You are losing this exchange, so change what the ball looks like before you change where it goes; height and weight cost nothing and push an early taker back. Ripping down the line is the classic escape and the classic error.
takeaway: Change ball quality before ball direction.
mistakeType: line gamble to escape a losing exchange

scenario: You change ends at 3–2 and now you're hitting into a stiff wind. Your last two flat drives died a metre inside the baseline, and she's floating replies from well behind hers.
options: Swing full and aim near the lines
Add spin and aim well inside the lines
Take pace off and keep it safe
explanation: A headwind brakes and holds every ball, so full swings land short of the lines you would normally fear; this is the set to attack. Adding spin and margin is the with-the-wind answer, and into the wind it just feeds her short balls.
takeaway: Into the wind, swing free; with it, add spin.

scenario: 4–4 in the third and you have just gone to her backhand corner again. She has sent eleven of her last twelve backhands crosscourt from there, including on both break points.
options: Shade a step toward her crosscourt reply
Recover to the bisector of her two angles
Guard the line she has been ignoring
explanation: The bisector is the honest default, but eleven of twelve is evidence, not a hunch, and one step costs almost nothing on the rare change of direction. Guarding the line pays for a shot she has hit once all match.
takeaway: Respect the bisector, then lean where the evidence is.
mistakeType: baseline war of attrition vs a pusher

scenario: 30–30 and they float a short ball that lands near your service line and sits up. All match you've stopped, planted and floated these back from mid-court while they strolled back into position.
options: Move through it and follow it in
Plant, hit it hard, and stay back
Let it drop lower, then drive it
explanation: A mid-court ball is a transition ball: momentum through contact adds free pace and leaves you at the net for the reply. Planting and staying back is exactly what has been floating them back all match.
takeaway: Let your feet finish the short ball, not your arm.

scenario: 3–3, 30–15. Their slice lands short in your deuce court and you step inside the baseline while they recover to the centre. Their backhand has been a floating chip all match.
options: Approach down the line to the backhand
Approach crosscourt to the open court
Approach deep down the middle
explanation: The line approach travels the shorter distance and points you straight at the chip backhand, so you can shade the line and cover the pass. Crosscourt into the open court feels bigger but leaves the line pass behind you.
takeaway: Approach down the line, then shade the line.
mistakeType: crosscourt approaches that open the pass

focusTag: volleying against an opponent coming in
scenario: 15–30. Your volley landed short, they ran it down and are following their own reply in. You have a waist-high volley as they cross their service line.
options: Punch it at their feet
Angle it wide for the winner
Lob-volley it over their head
explanation: A moving opponent inside the box has to half-volley from below the tape, which hands you the ball you want next. The wide angle needs precision you do not have off waist height, and a short lob volley is a free overhead.
takeaway: Against an incoming opponent, volley at their shoelaces.
mistakeType: attempting an angled volley from too far back

focusTag: serve and volley on a second serve
scenario: 4–4, 30–30 on your second serve. They stand two metres behind the baseline and have chipped six of eight second-serve returns short and floating this set.
options: Kick it to the backhand and follow it in
Kick it to the backhand and hold the baseline
Go flat and hard down the T instead
explanation: A returner standing two metres back and chipping gives you a slow high ball at the service line, which is the return worth following. Holding the baseline turns that floater into a neutral rally you had already won the start of.
takeaway: A deep chip returner is an invitation — follow the serve in.

focusTag: volley target against a full sprint
scenario: 30–30. You have an easy volley at chest height. They are at a dead sprint across the baseline toward the open court, eyes on the sideline and two steps from reaching it.
options: Behind them, back where they came from
Into the open court they are sprinting to
Deep down the middle at their feet
explanation: At full sprint their weight is committed, and reversing costs two steps they do not have, so the ball behind them is untouchable. The open court is right once they have stopped and turned back toward the centre, not while they are running.
takeaway: Hit behind runners, into space against stoppers.
mistakeType: always hitting to the open court

focusTag: overhead target when you are moving back
scenario: 30–30, still air. Their lob pushes you back behind the service line, but you get around it in balance with the racket up and contact over your shoulder.
options: Smash deep through the middle and re-close
Flatten it into the open corner
Angle it short crosscourt with touch
explanation: A retreating overhead loses margin, so depth through the middle takes their angles away and lets you close in for an easier second one. The flat corner is the version that clips the tape or the line from that far back.
takeaway: Overhead from deep: deep and middle.

focusTag: when the wind makes you let it bounce
scenario: 5–4, 30–30 in a gusting crosswind. They throw up a very high, very deep lob that is still drifting as it falls, and you can get under it in time.
options: Let it bounce, then smash it deep
Take it in the air on the way down
Let it bounce and drive it deep
explanation: In still air you take a lob you can reach in balance, but a ball falling from that height in gusts keeps moving until contact, and the bounce hands you set feet. Taking it in the air there is a timing gamble on a big point.
takeaway: High, deep and windy: bounce it, then smash it.

scenario: 40–15, you're two metres from the net with a floater arriving at chest height. They just chased a deep ball and are still back-pedalling well behind the baseline.
options: Drop it short over the low net
Punch it deep into the open corner
Angle it wide past the sideline
explanation: Two metres from the net with contact above the tape, the drop travels barely a metre and their momentum is already going the wrong way. Punching deep is right from the service line, but here it feeds a player parked back there.
takeaway: Drop only when you're close in and they're going backwards.
mistakeType: drop volleys against a ready opponent

scenario: You've approached deep to the backhand corner and closed in behind it. It's 30–30 and they have already lobbed you twice this set from that corner. Where do you stop?
options: Stop 2–3 metres from the net, in the box
Close right in, a metre off the net
Hold at the service line and volley
explanation: Two to three metres in is the only band that still reaches the dipping ball yet lets you turn and run down a lob. Crowding the net is tempting after a good approach, but against someone already lobbing you it invites the same shot.
takeaway: Own the middle of the box, not the net cord.

focusTag: the job of a volley below net height
scenario: 3–4, 15–15. You are inside the box but their dipping crosscourt forces you to volley from below the tape, and they are set and balanced on the baseline behind it.
options: Lift it deep down the middle and split again
Carve a short angle crosscourt winner
Drop it short since it is already low
explanation: Below the tape you have to hit up, so depth through the middle keeps a balanced opponent behind the baseline and earns you the volley you actually want. The short angle from down there clears the net by nothing.
takeaway: Low volley: survive deep now, finish the next one.

focusTag: which balls not to follow in
scenario: 1–1 in the third, they slide a low skidding slice that dies short and you have to scoop it up from below net height. They're balanced on the baseline and have passed you twice off this exact ball.
options: Lift it deep and stay back
Follow it in and close the net
Chip it short and sprint forward
explanation: A ball lifted from below the net arrives slow and rising, so staying back keeps the rally neutral instead of handing them a target. Following it in is the habit that has already cost you two points against a balanced passer.
takeaway: Approach behind balls that hurt them, not ones that hurried you.

scenario: 1–1 in the third, 30–0 on their serve. Their second serve has sat up chest high and landed inside the service line all match, and they recover slowly behind it.
options: Chip it deep and follow it in
Rip a flat drive return and stay back
Block it deep and hold the baseline
explanation: A short chest-high second serve is the invitation: the chip stays low, buys the time to reach the box, and a slow recoverer must pass you from behind. Ripping a flat drive risks the miss and leaves you where they are comfortable.
takeaway: Short second serve, chip it deep and come in behind it.

scenario: 30–30, you're inside the service box and their lob comes up short, floating above your backhand shoulder. They've stopped in the middle of the baseline to watch it.
options: Punch it deep down the line
Angle it short with soft hands
Swing hard to end it there
explanation: The high backhand volley has no natural power, so a firm punch deep down the line is the version that stays honest and keeps them pinned. The soft short angle is the fashionable choice and the one that dumps into the net.
takeaway: High backhand volley: punch it deep, don't paint it.
mistakeType: getting cute on high backhand volleys

scenario: 40–30. Their defensive ball floats to you at shoulder height inside the baseline while they scramble back from the deuce corner, still four metres from the centre.
options: Swinging volley into the open court
Let it bounce and drive it hard
Punch it as a normal volley
explanation: Taking it out of the air removes the second and a half they need to get back, and shoulder height inside the baseline is where that swing is safe. Letting it bounce hands a scrambling opponent exactly the time they are chasing.
takeaway: Shoulder-high floater inside the baseline: take it early.

focusTag: reading the pass at the net
scenario: 30–30, you're two metres from the net and they're set up balanced for the pass. You've lunged early all set and twice they've changed direction at the last instant.
options: Split-step and move after contact
Lean to the open side before they swing
Back up a step to buy reaction time
explanation: Reading the ball off their strings is slower but never wrong, and from two metres in you can still reach both passing lanes. Leaning early is why they've beaten you twice: a late changer only needs to see you move first.
takeaway: Move after their contact, never before it.
